extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in physics, mechanics, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for doing and judging work in mechanics and physical science: how to form hypotheses, treat abstractions, relate mechanics to other branches (electricity, heat, physiology), and avoid metaphysical excesses. Emphasizes economy of thought, empirical test, and comparative concepts across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mathematical possibility from physical reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts (e.g., multi-dimensional spaces) are 'purely things of thought' and do not by themselves establish physical existence; the question whether experiential space has additional dimensions must be decided by experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat mathematical constructions as physical truths without empirical evidence. Example/antipattern: spiritualists using a 'fourth dimension' to explain tricks or metaphysical claims; such uses are fabrication when unsupported by observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat hypotheses as mental expedients, not substitutes for phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are helpful mental devices for explaining new phenomena but are 'nothing whatever to do with the phenomenon itself' unless supported by tangible, verifiable observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypotheses to guide inquiry, but avoid taking them as ontological commitments. Avoid piling up hypotheses that replace observed relations with equally numerous conjectures; expect no more enlightenment from a hypothesis than from the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict formulations to observable, quantitative elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Express physical conditions in terms of measurable quantities (e.g., potential function values, dielectric constants) rather than invoking unmeasured fluids or media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: eliminate 'fluids' in electricity theory by using potential function and dielectric constants; prefer derived notions (Q, Φ) as secondary to directly measurable values. This fosters economy and avoids imaginary problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the artificiality of purely mechanical abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely mechanical phenomena are idealizations; in nature mechanical effects are always associated with thermal, magnetic, electrical, and chemical phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mechanical models as abstractions made for comprehension; don't mistake them for isolated physical realities. Be explicit when neglecting other interacting aspects for the sake of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume historical precedence implies fundamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that some knowledge (e.g., mechanics) was discovered earlier does not prove it is the foundation of all later discoveries; earlier laws need not be the deepest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of claims that mechanics is the basis of all physics simply because it developed earlier. Remain open to new ideas of general scope arising from later discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue comparative physics: find correspondences across domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove notions rooted in historical or conventional accident by comparing conceptions across departments (e.g., temperatures ↔ velocities, thermal capacities ↔ masses, potential of electric charge ↔ quantity of heat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies to build a homogeneous physics that concisely expresses large groups of facts without arbitrary additions. This comparative approach aids economy of thought and conceptual unification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor economy of thought over speculative substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting a hypothesis that reproduces phenomena substitutes factual relations with an equal number of hypotheses, which is not necessarily an intellectual gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer minimal assumptions; once a hypothesis has served to clarify facts, do not expect it to continue yielding deeper truths beyond the observed relations it helped reveal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of causality and equivalence of cause and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of nature are equations between measurable elements; effects are dependent on causes, and the 'equivalence of cause and effect' implies reversible mapping of groups of circumstances under transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate laws as relations among measurable quantities. Use the concept to understand reciprocal phenomena (e.g., Seebeck ↔ Peltier), and recognize constraints (periodic cause → periodic effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation (economy) as a methodological principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of conservation (e.g., conservation of energy) have a firm foundation in the economy of thought: identify quantities that remain constant to facilitate mental reconstruction of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conservation laws as statements of invariable quantitative connections among phenomena rather than metaphysical truths. Avoid extending conservation principles beyond the domain where repetitions and measurements justify them (e.g., universe-as-whole cautions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical mysticism attached to scientific principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific principles like conservation are abstractions based on repeated similar cases; metaphysical or mystical readings (e.g., cosmic metaphysics from conservation) are unwarranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep scientific laws within empirical and methodological contexts. Example antipattern: treating conservation as proof of a metaphysical 'substance' or applying it absurdly to the entire universe without repeatable cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain connection between specialized science and life needs
rubrics_metrics.description: All science originates in the needs of life; each branch attains best development by living connection with the whole to avoid lop-sided or monstrous growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While specialization is necessary, retain interdisciplinary awareness so that specialized instruments do not become ends in themselves detached from practical or biological contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reify intellectual instruments as objective reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts such as mass, force, and atom are intellectual implements to represent experiences economically, not necessarily independent objects of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mistaking models or representational devices for the 'real world' mechanism. Example: just because the theatre has a machine-room does not imply the world has an analogous machine-room; distinguish representation from ontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require philosophical perspective for special investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators must have a philosophy of the relations of special knowledge to general knowledge to avoid formulating absurd problems (e.g., 'can feelings be explained by motions of atoms?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical reflection prevents category mistakes and helps frame sensible, solvable problems. Lack of such perspective manifests in the enunciation of imaginary or ill-posed problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat mechanical quantities as ordinal symbols of sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical quantities are ordinal symbols representing members of well-ordered sets of sensations (space, time, touch, sight); equations express forms of interdependence among these symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this view to avoid unsupported reductionism (e.g., deriving sensations directly from atomic motions). Recognize the representational role of equations rather than viewing them as literal generators of sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize multi-aspect nature of processes (physics ↔ physiology)
rubrics_metrics.description: An element (e.g., heat of body A) is connected with other physical elements and with aggregates of elements of our bodies (nerves); processes that appear purely mechanical are simultaneously physiological, electrical, chemical, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid analyzing phenomena solely within one departmental frame when multiple facets are intrinsically present; treat disciplines as aspects of the same event, and be cautious in neglecting complementary aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict expositions to actual facts to avoid false problems
rubrics_metrics.description: If means and aims of research are properly distinguished and expositions restricted to presenting actual facts, false or imaginary problems cannot arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame scientific writings and arguments around observable facts and their measured relations; avoid speculative constructions that conflate representation levels or invent insoluble problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret conservation laws as expressions of quantitative connection, not mechanistic causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws like vis viva (conservation of energy) state an invariable quantitative connection between different kinds of phenomena (mechanical, thermal, electrical) rather than implying mechanics is the causal basis of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conservation statements descriptively to connect measurable quantities across phenomena, and resist mechanistic over-interpretation that would elevate one class of phenomena as fundamentally causal of all others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise care in inverting dependencies and generalizing relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When reasoning about cause-effect inversions, respect the form of dependence: a perceptible alteration of a may be produced by altering A, but changing A need not produce a change in a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when inferring reciprocal relations; use concrete examples (e.g., Faraday induction relations) to test whether inversions are valid in form and scope.
